t: The number of different ways in which 2 lives can be selected from a group of 5 lives is:
e: The number of combinations is ⁵C₂ = 5!/(2! 3!) = 10; order of selection does not matter.

t: Given l₅₀ = 90,000 and l₆₀ = 80,000, the probability that a life now aged 30, who is known to have survived to age 50, also survives to age 60 is approximately:
e: Given survival to 50, the conditional probability is ₁₀p₅₀ = l₆₀/l₅₀ = 80,000/90,000 ≈ 0.889; the history before age 50 is irrelevant.

t: Three independent lives each have a one-year survival probability of 0.8. The probability that exactly two of them survive the year is:
₹1,000 is payable at the end of 2 years provided a life aged x is then alive. If ₂pₓ = 0.9 and v² = 0.9, the expected present value is:
An indicator variable takes the value 1 if a life dies within the year (probability 0.1) and 0 otherwise. Its variance is:
e: For a Bernoulli variable Var = q(1 − q) = 0.1 × 0.9 = 0.09.

t: A fund earned 10% in year 1 and 20% in year 2. Given √1.32 = 1.149, the average (geometric mean) annual rate of return is approximately:
e: The geometric mean rate solves (1 + g)² = 1.1 × 1.2 = 1.32, so g = 1.149 − 1 = 14.9%, slightly less than the arithmetic mean of 15%.

t: A population has variance 100. The variance of the mean of a random sample of 25 independent observations is:
e: Var(sample mean) = σ²/n = 100/25 = 4; the standard error of the mean is therefore 2.

t: The median of the observations 4, 8, 10 and 14 is:
e: With an even number of ordered observations the median is the average of the two middle values: (8 + 10)/2 = 9.

t: At 10% per annum simple interest, ₹1,000 will grow to ₹1,500 in:
e: Interest required = ₹500 = 1,000 × 0.10 × t, so t = 5 years. Under compound interest it would take a little over 4 years.

t: ₹50,000 is invested at 8% per annum compound for 3 years. Given (1.08)³ = 1.2597, the accumulated amount is approximately:
₹10,000 is invested at 10% per annum simple interest. The accumulated amount after 3 years is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Simple interest is charged only on the principal: 10,000 × 0.10 × 3 = ₹3,000, giving an amount of ₹13,000.

t: ₹10,000 is invested for one year at a nominal rate of 12% per annum convertible monthly. Given (1.01)¹² = 1.1268, the amount at the end of the year is:
e: Each month earns 1%, so the amount is 10,000 × (1.01)¹² = 10,000 × 1.1268 = ₹11,268, more than ₹11,200 under 12% effective.

t: If the discount factor v = 0.9, the present value of three payments of ₹1,000 due at the end of 1, 2 and 3 years respectively is:
Under a constant force of interest of 10% per annum (e^−0.1 = 0.9048), the present value of ₹10,000 due in one year is:
At 4% per annum, v = 0.9615 and v² = 0.9246. The value of a₂ is:
For a life aged 40, D₄₀ = 2,000, N₄₁ = 30,000 and N₅₁ = 14,000. The value of a 10-year temporary life annuity-immediate a₄₀:₁₀ is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). a₄₀:₁₀ = (N₄₁ − N₅₁)/D₄₀ = (30,000 − 14,000)/2,000 = 8.

t: A loan of ₹1,00,000 is to be repaid by 20 level annual instalments in arrear at 8% per annum. Given a₂₀ at 8% = 9.8181, each instalment is approximately:
At 5% per annum, a₁₀ = 7.7217 and v¹⁰ = 0.6139. The difference ä₁₀ − a₁₀ equals:
e: ä₁₀ − a₁₀ = 1 − v¹⁰ = 1 − 0.6139 = 0.3861: the annuity-due has an extra payment now but lacks the payment at time 10.

t: At 10% per annum (v = 0.9091, v² = 0.8264, v³ = 0.7513), the present value of payments of ₹1, ₹2 and ₹3 at the ends of years 1, 2 and 3 respectively is approximately:
A loan of ₹20,000 at 10% per annum is repaid by two equal annual instalments in arrear. Given a₂ at 10% = 1.7355, each instalment is approximately:
The present value of a continuously payable annuity of 1 per annum for n years, āₙ, is given by:
e: āₙ = (1 − vⁿ)/δ, using the force of interest in the denominator, whereas aₙ uses i and äₙ uses d.

t: A life table has a radix l₀ = 1,00,000 and l₁ = 99,000. The infant mortality rate q₀ is:
Given ₁₀p₄₀ = 0.95 and q₅₀ = 0.004, the probability that a life aged 40 dies between ages 50 and 51 is:
For a certain age lₓ = 90,000 and Tₓ = 27,00,000. The complete expectation of life e°ₓ and the approximate curtate expectation eₓ are respectively:
e: e°ₓ = Tₓ/lₓ = 27,00,000/90,000 = 30 years, and eₓ ≈ e°ₓ − ½ = 29.5 years.

t: Given l₂₅ = 97,000 and l₆₅ = 72,750, the probability that a life aged 25 survives to the retirement age of 65 is:
Under De Moivre's law with limiting age ω = 100, lₓ is proportional to (100 − x). The probability that a life aged 40 survives to age 60 is:
In a stationary population with 1,000 births per year and a complete expectation of life at birth of 70 years, the total population is:
e: In a stationary population the total size equals (annual births) × e°₀ = 1,000 × 70 = 70,000, since births equal deaths and the age distribution is constant.

t: A prize scheme pays ₹1,000 with probability 0.1, ₹100 with probability 0.3 and nothing otherwise. The expected payout is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). E = 1,000 × 0.1 + 100 × 0.3 + 0 × 0.6 = 100 + 30 = ₹130.

t: In a double decrement table with deaths and withdrawals, the total rate of decrement (aq)ₓ equals:
o: the product of the dependent rates of death and withdrawal
the sum of the dependent rates (aq)ᵈₓ + (aq)ʷₓ
the independent rate of mortality qₓ only
e: All exits from the table are counted, so the total decrement rate is the sum of the dependent (table) rates for each cause; independent rates cannot simply be added.

t: A retiree aged 65 is to receive a pension of ₹1,20,000 per annum, payable at the end of each year for life. If ä₆₅ = 10, the value of the pension is:
e: Payments in arrear use a₆₅ = ä₆₅ − 1 = 9, so the value is 1,20,000 × 9 = ₹10,80,000.

t: Given N₃₀ = 60,000, N₆₀ = 10,000 and D₃₀ = 2,500, the 30-year temporary life annuity-due ä₃₀:₃₀ is:
For a life aged x, äₓ = 18 and the n-year temporary annuity-due äₓ:ₙ = 12. The n-year deferred whole life annuity-due ₙ|äₓ is:
e: A whole life annuity splits into a temporary part and a deferred part: ₙ|äₓ = äₓ − äₓ:ₙ = 18 − 12 = 6.

t: If äₓ = 13, the approximate value of the annuity-due payable monthly äₓ⁽¹²⁾ (using äₓ⁽ᵐ⁾ ≈ äₓ − (m − 1)/2m) is:
e: äₓ⁽¹²⁾ ≈ äₓ − 11/24 = 13 − 0.4583 = 12.54; monthly payments in advance are received on average later than one annual payment in advance.

t: If äₓ:ₙ = 12 and ₙEₓ = 0.4, the n-year temporary life annuity-immediate aₓ:ₙ is:
e: aₓ:ₙ = äₓ:ₙ − 1 + ₙEₓ = 12 − 1 + 0.4 = 11.4: drop the payment at time 0 and add the payment at time n made on survival.

t: Given M₄₀ = 600 and D₄₀ = 2,500, the whole life assurance A₄₀ (benefit at the end of the year of death) is:
Under the IRDAI (Protection of Policyholders' Interests) Regulations 2024, the free-look period for a policy with a term of one year or more is:
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). 30 days from receipt of the policy document, irrespective of the sales channel.

t: Which of the following statements about a whole life assurance of ₹1 on (x) is INCORRECT?
o: Aₓ increases with the age x
Āₓ (payable immediately on death) is greater than Aₓ (payable at the end of the year of death)
Aₓ increases when a higher rate of interest is used
e: A higher rate of interest discounts the future benefit more heavily, so Aₓ decreases, not increases. The other three statements are correct.

t: If A₄₀ = 0.24, the net single premium for a whole life assurance of ₹10,00,000 on a life aged 40 is:
For a life aged x, the n-year endowment assurance Aₓ:ₙ = 0.52 and the n-year term assurance A¹ₓ:ₙ = 0.07. The n-year pure endowment ₙEₓ is:
e: Endowment = term + pure endowment, so ₙEₓ = 0.52 − 0.07 = 0.45.

t: A family income benefit policy provides, on death of the life assured within the term:
o: a lump sum equal to total premiums paid
an income payable from death until the end of the original term
a lump sum payable at the end of the term
an income for the lifetime of the beneficiary
e: The benefit is a regular income running from the date of death to the end of the selected term, so the amount of cover falls as the term progresses, like a decreasing term assurance.

t: Given D₃₀ = 2,500 and D₆₀ = 625, the 30-year pure endowment factor ₃₀E₃₀ is:
In commutation notation, the ratio Nₓ / Dₓ represents:
e: Nₓ/Dₓ = äₓ, the annuity-due; aₓ = Nₓ₊₁/Dₓ and Aₓ = Mₓ/Dₓ.

t: Given M₄₀ = 600 and M₄₁ = 580, the value of C₄₀ is:
e: Mₓ = Cₓ + Mₓ₊₁, so C₄₀ = M₄₀ − M₄₁ = 600 − 580 = 20.

t: For a whole life assurance of ₹1,000 on a life aged 40 with premiums payable throughout life, A₄₀ = 0.24 and ä₄₀ = 19. The net annual premium is approximately:
An Insurance Ombudsman can entertain a complaint where the value of the claim, including expenses, does not exceed:
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). The limit was raised to ₹50 lakh by the amended Insurance Ombudsman Rules.

t: For an n-year term assurance of ₹1,000, A¹ₓ:ₙ = 0.084 and äₓ:ₙ = 14. The net annual premium is:
Which of the following is treated as an initial expense when loading the office premium?
o: First-year agency commission and medical examination fees
e: Initial expenses are incurred once at the inception of the policy (commission, underwriting, medical reports, policy issue), unlike renewal, claim and investment expenses which recur.

t: A life aged 50 purchases an annuity of ₹1,00,000 per annum, payable in arrear for life, commencing at age 60. If ₁₀|a₅₀ = 5.5, the single premium is:
For a whole life assurance with net premiums payable for life, äₓ = 15 and äₓ₊ₜ = 12. Using ₜVₓ = 1 − äₓ₊ₜ/äₓ, the net premium reserve at duration t per ₹1 is:
A whole life policy for ₹5,00,000 has a net premium reserve of 0.20 per ₹1 sum assured. If the insurer pays a surrender value equal to the reserve less a 10% surrender charge, the surrender value is:
e: Reserve = 5,00,000 × 0.20 = ₹1,00,000; less 10% gives a surrender value of ₹90,000.
